mcqs.learning_point: Meaning of matter at the introductory level
mcqs.question: Which of the following best defines matter?

options.A: Anything that has mass and occupies space.

mcqs.answer: Anything that has mass and occupies space.
mcqs.explanation: Matter is defined as anything that has mass and takes up space. Option A states this definition correctly. Option B limits matter to solids, which is false. Option C ignores liquids, gases and invisible matter. Option D confuses matter with energy.

mcqs.learning_point: Examples of matter in everyday life
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of matter?
mcqs.explanation: Matter must have mass and occupy space. Sunlight is electromagnetic radiation (energy) and does not have mass, so it is not matter. The other three items are tangible substances that have mass and volume.

mcqs.learning_point: Different forms in which matter is encountered
mcqs.question: Matter can be found in which three main states?
mcqs.explanation: At the introductory level for Class 6, matter is described in three familiar states: solid, liquid and gas. While plasma and other exotic states exist, they are beyond the scope of this curriculum. Hence option A is correct; the other options include states not taught at this level or mix terms incorrectly.

mcqs.learning_point: Meaning of matter at the introductory level
mcqs.question: A ball is placed on a table. Which statement best shows the concept of matter?

options.A: The ball can be seen because it reflects light.
options.B: The ball has mass and takes up space on the table.
options.C: The ball is moving because of gravity.

mcqs.answer: The ball has mass and takes up space on the table.
mcqs.explanation: The definition of matter emphasizes mass and volume. Option B directly mentions both properties, demonstrating the concept. Option A talks about visibility, which is not part of the definition. Option C describes motion, and option D mentions temperature—neither defines matter.

mcqs.learning_point: Examples of matter in everyday life
mcqs.question: Which group lists only things that are matter?
mcqs.explanation: Air, water and rock are all substances that have mass and occupy space, fitting the definition of matter. The items in options B, C and D are forms of energy or sensations, not matter.

mcqs.learning_point: Different forms in which matter is encountered
mcqs.question: A child sees ice, water, and steam. Which form of matter does each represent?

options.A: Ice – solid, water – liquid, steam – gas
options.B: Ice – gas, water – solid, steam – liquid
options.C: Ice – liquid, water – gas, steam – solid

mcqs.answer: Ice – solid, water – liquid, steam – gas
mcqs.explanation: Ice is the solid form of water, liquid water is the liquid form, and steam (water vapor) is the gaseous form. Options B, C and D incorrectly assign states.

mcqs.learning_point: Meaning of matter at the introductory level
mcqs.question: Which statement reflects a common misconception about matter?

options.A: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
options.B: Matter can be created or destroyed easily.
options.C: Matter includes solids, liquids, and gases.

mcqs.answer: Matter can be created or destroyed easily.
mcqs.explanation: The law of conservation of matter states that matter cannot be created or destroyed in ordinary physical processes. Option B is therefore a misconception. Options A, C and D are correct statements about matter.

mcqs.learning_point: Examples of matter in everyday life
mcqs.question: A student says the smell of perfume is not matter because it cannot be seen. Which reasoning is correct?

options.A: The perfume is matter because it has mass and occupies space even if invisible.
options.B: The perfume is not matter because only visible things are matter.
options.C: The perfume is energy, not matter.
options.D: The perfume is a feeling, not matter.

mcqs.answer: The perfume is matter because it has mass and occupies space even if invisible.
mcqs.explanation: Perfume consists of tiny particles that have mass and take up space, satisfying the definition of matter, even though they may be invisible. Options B, C and D incorrectly equate visibility or sensation with the definition of matter.
